text.title: Rust Ownership Core Rules
text.summary: 11 testable rules for signature design — questions to answer, defaults to prefer, escape hatches to avoid, plus the terminal skip guard.

rule.statement: Each value has exactly one owner at a time. Transfer ownership with a move; never with `.clone()`.

rationale.source: Rust Book ch.4; v1-source + faion-net curation

rule.rationale: Cloning to hand a value onward copies the data and obscures who is responsible for the drop — the reader can no longer tell which copy is the live one.

rule.statement: At any point a value has either many shared borrows (`&T`) or exactly one exclusive borrow (`&mut T`) — never both. Design scopes so the two never overlap.

rationale.source: Rust Book ch.4; v1-source + faion-net curation

rule.rationale: This is the aliasing guarantee the whole model rests on; the borrow checker rejects the overlap precisely because it would be undefined behaviour in C.

rule.statement: Before writing any function body, document the answers to three questions in a comment above the signature: (1) does this function need to keep the value after returning? (2) does it modify the value? (3) does it need to share the value across threads or with another scope? Skipping the audit is forbidden.

rationale.source: Rust Book ch.4; klabnik — Rust for Rustaceans

rule.rationale: Most borrow-checker pain stems from a wrong signature. Body-first design produces `.clone()` propagation. Signature-first design picks the right shape immediately.

rule.statement: Default to `&T` for read-only parameters. `String` → `&str`, `Vec<T>` → `&[T]`, `PathBuf` → `&Path`. Only take ownership when the function actually consumes the value (stores it in a struct, returns it, drops it).
rule.rationale: `&str`/`&[T]`/`&Path` accept more callers (string literals, vec slices) at zero cost. Taking `String` forces every caller to `.to_string()` or `.clone()`.

rule.statement: Use `&mut T` only when the function modifies the value. If only one branch needs mutation, restructure: take `&T` and `match` to a path that returns an owned modification.
rule.rationale: `&mut T` blocks all other access for its lifetime. Adding it speculatively forces callers to release other borrows even when no mutation happens.

rule.statement: `Rc<RefCell<T>>` is an escape hatch, not a default. Reach for it only when the data structure is genuinely a graph with cycles. For tree-shaped data use `Box<T>` + parent pointer-by-id. For state machines use enum + ownership move.

rationale.source: Rust Book ch.15; The Rust Reference Counter

rule.rationale: `Rc<RefCell>` defers borrow checks to runtime and produces panics or silent aliasing bugs. The borrow checker is not the enemy — fight it by redesigning the data, not by hiding it.

rule.statement: `Arc<T>` only when the value crosses a thread boundary (spawned thread, async task, `tokio::spawn`). Single-threaded shared ownership uses `Rc<T>` (cheaper). Synchronous code with no `Send` requirement does not need `Arc`.
rule.rationale: `Arc` uses atomic refcount ops; `Rc` uses non-atomic. Wrapping single-threaded data in `Arc` pays the atomic cost on every clone for no safety benefit.

rule.statement: `Rc<T>` and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` MUST NOT cross a thread boundary — no `std::thread::spawn`, no `tokio::spawn`, no `rayon` closure. Shared mutable state that crosses threads uses `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or `Arc<RwLock<T>>`.
rule.rationale: `Rc` and `RefCell` are `!Send` and `!Sync` — their refcount and borrow flag are non-atomic, so sharing them across threads is a data race. The compiler catches the direct case, but the reflexive workaround (wrapping in `unsafe impl Send`, or restructuring until the bound disappears) breaks soundness silently.

rule.statement: Calling `.clone()` purely to silence the borrow checker is forbidden. Fix the signature instead: lift the value into a longer-lived scope, take a borrow, or split the call site so two mutable borrows do not overlap. A clone that survives review carries a comment stating why.
rule.rationale: `.clone()` compiles, so it feels like a fix; what it actually does is convert a design question into an allocation on a hot path and leave the ownership story unreadable for the next person.

rule.statement: If lifetime elision rules (Rust Reference ch.10) apply, omit lifetimes. If they don't, write the explicit lifetime AND a comment naming what outlives what. Never just add `'static` to silence the compiler.
rule.rationale: `'static` is rarely what you mean. The compiler suggests it as the safest fallback; accepting silently forces all callers to also pin `'static`, propagating the wrong constraint.

rule.statement: A crate whose hot paths matter runs `templates/audit-clones.sh` in CI: clippy with `redundant_clone`, `needless_clone`, `clone_on_copy` and `implicit_clone` warned, plus a clone-count baseline that a PR may not regress without a stated reason.
rule.rationale: Per-signature discipline decays between reviews. A counted baseline turns "we prefer borrows" from a shared intention into a number a diff either holds or explains.

rule.statement: If the preconditions in `Applies If` fail or any `Skip If` condition holds — a throwaway script, a proc macro, an FFI wrapper, generated code, or embedded code with no heap — return `skipped` and apply no further rules.
rule.rationale: Methodologies are not universal; enforcing signature-first ownership on generated `prost` code or a token-stream macro fights the ecosystem and produces churn instead of safety.
